title: How Anushka Sharma Turned Virat Kohli Into India's Most Famous Vegetarian
excerpt: The cricketer's plant-based pivot, inspired by his wife, reflects a broader shift in how diaspora Indians think about food, faith, and performance.
body:
In the hypercompetitive world of international cricket, where sports nutritionists obsess over macros and recovery windows, Virat Kohli has made an improbable dietary choice: he has gone vegetarian. More improbable still, the man once synonymous with Delhi's butter-chicken machismo credits his wife, Anushka Sharma, with the transformation — calling it one of the best decisions of his life.

The revelation, shared in a recent interview, is more than celebrity gossip. It sits at the intersection of two powerful currents in contemporary Indian culture: the wellness revolution sweeping India's urban middle class, and the spiritual turn that has made ashram retreats, meditation apps, and conscious eating mainstream aspirations.

## From Non-Veg to No-Veg

Kohli's dietary shift was neither overnight nor performative. In earlier interviews, the batsman had spoken of experimenting with a vegan diet around 2018, partly for athletic performance and partly on ethical grounds. He later reintroduced some dairy but remained firmly vegetarian — a distinction that matters in India, where the line between vegetarianism and veganism carries cultural, caste, and religious weight.

Sharma, who had already adopted a vegetarian lifestyle before their marriage, was the catalyst. "She made me see the connection between what you eat and how you feel — not just physically, but in terms of empathy," Kohli said. The couple has maintained their plant-based household through gruelling cricket tours, finding vegetarian options from Barbados to Brisbane. Their go-to meals reportedly range from gluten-free pho to Delhi-style chole bhature — a reassuring reminder that vegetarianism need not mean deprivation.

## The Spiritual Thread

The dietary change is part of a broader philosophical shift. Kohli and Sharma have been photographed at ashrams in Rishikesh, meditating at retreats linked to Swami Dayanand Saraswati, and speaking openly about ego, gratitude, and inner peace — themes that would have drawn mockery in Indian cricket's old guard. Spiritual teacher Jaya Kishori publicly praised the couple, noting that "even those who have everything still need peace to find balance."

For NRIs, this spiritual-wellness packaging matters. It offers a modern, cosmopolitan frame for dietary choices that previous generations defended in purely religious terms. When a young Indian-American professional declines a steak at a client dinner, invoking Kohli's performance-driven vegetarianism lands differently than invoking grandparental tradition.

## India's Plant-Based Moment

Kohli's influence arrives at a time when India's relationship with vegetarianism is itself in flux. The country has long had one of the world's largest vegetarian populations — roughly 30-40% by most estimates — but the reasons are shifting. Where caste and religious identity once drove the choice, health consciousness, environmental concern, and animal welfare now compete for primacy, particularly among younger, urban Indians.

The market has followed. India's plant-based food sector was valued at over $800 million in 2024, with companies like GoodDot, Imagine Meats (co-founded by Genelia and Riteish Deshmukh), and Blue Tribe seeing double-digit growth. In diaspora hubs — New Jersey, the Bay Area, Southall, Brampton — Indian restaurants increasingly market "plant-forward" menus that would have been unthinkable a decade ago.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, Kohli's public vegetarianism does something subtle but significant: it decouples Indian dietary practice from the apologetic tone that has sometimes accompanied it in Western settings. When India's most celebrated athlete — not a yoga guru, not a religious leader, but a fast-bowler-punishing, record-breaking cricketer — says plants fuel his performance, it shifts the conversation.

The effect is amplified by Sharma's parallel influence as an actor and entrepreneur. Together, they present a template that is aspirational without being preachy — health-conscious, spiritually grounded, and entirely comfortable in global settings.

Whether Kohli's diet actually improves his batting average is a question best left to sports scientists. What is clear is that his willingness to speak about it publicly, crediting his wife rather than a nutritionist or a brand deal, has given India's vegetarian tradition its most charismatic modern ambassador — and given millions of NRIs one more reason to feel that their kitchen table is, in fact, ahead of the curve.
